promptText:
Role/Reference: Paint this the way a Studio Ghibli background artist in the Kazuo Oga tradition (lead background painter for Miyazaki's My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, Spirited Away) would build a feature-film establishing plate — a traditional gouache-and-watercolor background painting meant to hold up as a standalone frame, not a cel-shaded character illustration.

Technical reference (traditional anime background-painting method): Ghibli backgrounds are built in physical media — gouache and watercolor on paper — with a deliberate difference in brush handling by depth: soft, wet washes for sky and distant hills (where paint is thinned and blended for atmospheric softness) versus drier, more textured, individually-visible brushstrokes for foreground grass and foliage (where the paint is applied more directly, leaving visible strokes). This isn't just style — it's the same atmospheric-perspective principle real landscape photography uses, translated into paint handling: three genuine depth layers (crisp saturated foreground, softer slightly-desaturated midground, pale blue-shifted background) do the actual spatial work, exactly the way haze does in a photographed landscape. Cel-style flat shading — one clean shadow tone with a hard edge, no soft airbrush gradient — is the traditional 2D-animation convention for any foreground character or object, distinct from the painterly background technique. A low horizon line is a deliberate Ghibli compositional convention, giving the sky (and its clouds, doing emotional/weather work) the majority of the frame rather than the ground.

Subject: [A PEACEFUL COUNTRYSIDE SCENE] — rolling green hills stitched with a winding dirt path, a small traditional house with a red tile roof, a meadow scattered with wildflowers swaying in a light breeze, a distant tree line, and puffy cumulus clouds drifting across a bright blue sky.

Medium/technique: built up like a traditional gouache-and-watercolor background plate — soft blended washes for the sky and distant hills, drier and more textured individual brushwork for foreground grass and foliage, with hand-drawn imperfection running through every line (nothing perfectly straight or perfectly repeated, matching hand-painted production art rather than a vector illustration). Cel-style flat shading (one clean shadow tone, no soft gradients) on any foreground character or object. Three clear atmospheric depth layers: crisp, saturated, detailed foreground grass; slightly desaturated, softer-edged midground trees and house; pale, blue-shifted, near-flat background hills fading toward the horizon.

Lighting: warm late-afternoon sun raking low from camera-left, long soft-edged shadows stretching across the grass, a gentle golden-hour color cast warming every surface it touches — the luminous, slightly hazy glow associated with Oga's classic background paintings.

Palette: verdant greens across at least three distinct values, warm sunlit yellows in the light-struck grass, soft sky blues, and a single saturated pop of red on the roof as the color accent that anchors the composition.

Composition: staged in the classic Ghibli convention of a low horizon line giving the sky room to breathe; a wide establishing view with foreground-midground-background layering, the path acting as a leading line that carries the eye from the bottom of the frame back to the house.

Mood: nostalgic, unhurried — the quiet emotional warmth of a remembered summer afternoon rather than a dramatic moment.

Parameters: 16:9 aspect ratio, high detail, feature-film background-painting finish. --ar 16:9 --stylize 180 --niji 6 --no sharp vector lines, harsh black outlines, 3D render, photorealism, text, watermark.

Platform note: --niji 6 is Midjourney's anime/illustration-tuned model, sharper at Ghibli-style hand-painted backgrounds than the default --v model, which tends toward Western-illustration or photographic bias for this kind of brief. --stylize 180 sits low in Midjourney's 0-1000 range, staying close to the literal brief while still letting Niji's illustrative instincts through rather than flattening into a generic anime look.

promptText:
Style: an atmospheric anime illustration in the exact tradition of Makoto Shinkai's "Kimi no Na wa"/"Suzume" sky-as-subject staging — hyper-detailed, melancholic, engineered so the sky and its light do the emotional storytelling rather than the character's expression, which stays quiet and understated.

Subject: [A CHARACTER, e.g. a girl with long dark hair in a school uniform] standing alone on a Japanese train station platform at twilight, weight settled on one leg, gaze lifted very slightly toward the sky rather than at camera — a held, suspended-time stillness reading as the specific ache of a fleeting moment about to end, not posed drama.

Technique checklist (the load-bearing rules that make this read as Shinkai rather than generic anime-scenery):
1. LIGHT PHYSICS FIRST — every bloom, flare, or glow must trace to a real emitter (the low sun, a train headlamp, a platform lamp, a lit window). No decorative flares floating free of a source; this discipline is what separates Shinkai's restraint from generic light-leak filters.
2. THE SKY IS THE SUBJECT — hold at least the upper two-thirds of the frame for the sky's gradient and cloud structure; the character occupies the lower third at most, small enough that scale itself communicates solitude.
3. GRADIENT BANDING ORDER — zenith deep ultramarine blue → mid-sky violet/lavender → thin band of dusty rose → warm peach-gold hugging the horizon, each band blended, none banded with a hard edge.
4. MIRRORED SURFACES — every reflective plane (platform tile, rail head, glass) must echo the sky's actual gradient and cloud color, not a flat grey — this is one of the most-skipped details that breaks the illusion.
5. ATMOSPHERIC PERSPECTIVE — distant elements (far end of the platform, distant hills/rooftops) desaturate and cool slightly, a hazy value-compression that reads as genuine depth rather than flat layering.
6. RESTRAINT ON PARTICLES — dust motes and light particles suspended in the god-rays should be sparse and soft, never so dense they read as snow or confetti.

Medium/technique: hyper-detailed, near-photographic environmental rendering — accurate station architecture (platform edge tiles, signal wires, overhead catenary lines, a route sign in soft-focus background text), a single train approaching in the distance with warm glowing window light and a faint motion-soft edge, restrained anamorphic-style horizontal lens flare and soft bloom placed exactly at true light sources, fine dust and light particles suspended in the glow.

Visual qualities: a sweeping, carefully banded sky gradient (see banding order above) with individual cloud masses catching the last raking light along their undersides in warm coral, one first star just visible near the zenith, soft volumetric god-rays breaking through gaps in the clouds at a shallow angle consistent with a near-set sun. Palette: rich saturated blue-to-violet dominating roughly 60% of the frame against warm amber/peach highlights on the figure, train, and horizon (~30%), with one small saturated accent — a red signal light or a warm shopfront glow — reserved for visual anchoring (~10%). Pushed to a high dynamic range so deep shadow and bright sky coexist believably in one frame.

Background/composition: framed from a slightly low cinematic angle, camera near platform height, so the sky dominates the upper two-thirds — the hallmark Shinkai sky-as-emotional-subject staging. Deep foreground-to-background depth via strong linear perspective down the platform and converging rail lines, the figure kept small against the vast sky so scale carries the loneliness rather than facial expression.

Aspect ratio: 16:9 (cinematic widescreen). For a taller crop that pushes the sky even further, 9:16 also works well for the same brief with the platform compressed toward the bottom edge.

Negative / avoid: harsh unmotivated lens flares, flat single-tone sky, desaturated or muddy color, crowded platform with multiple background characters competing for focus, daytime lighting, photographic grain that reads as noise rather than dust, text/watermark/signature.

Consistency note: if this is one frame of a multi-panel sequence (e.g. a "before/after the train arrives" pair), keep the character description, camera height, and gradient banding order identical across prompts and vary only the train's position and the sky's exact color temperature — Midjourney does not guarantee an identical character across separate generations, so for a true matched pair generate both from the same prompt session back to back and pick the closest lighting match.

--ar 16:9 --niji 6 --style scenic --stylize 250

Platform note: tuned for Midjourney's --niji 6 (anime-tuned) model. For a slightly more painterly, less line-art-driven result, swap to --v 6.1 --style raw --stylize 200; the plain-language description above renders comparably in Nano Banana/Gemini image generation without any parameter suffix.

promptText:
Style: a loose, airy hand-painted botanical watercolor built on genuine wet-on-wet bloom-and-bleed physics — the elegant, gallery-quality look of a classical botanical print or a fine-art print/card line, not a digital "watercolor filter" pass.

Subject: [SUBJECT, e.g. a sprig of eucalyptus with a few wildflowers], with most detail, edge-definition, and pigment saturation concentrated at one focal cluster and progressively looser, softer-edged, and more diluted toward the stem tips — the classical botanical-plate convention of a single point of resolved focus.

Technique checklist (what makes this read as real watercolor rather than a vector illustration with a texture layer):
1. WET-ON-WET FIRST, DETAIL LAST — the underlying wash goes down loose and unpredictable (soft blooms, cauliflower edges where wet paint meets wet paint), and only the focal cluster receives later dry-brush and ink refinement over the dried wash.
2. LAYER COUNT — build color in 2-3 translucent glazes rather than one flat coat; each pass should let the one beneath show through, especially in shadow-side petals and leaf undersides.
3. GRANULATION — let pigment settle unevenly into the paper's tooth (the grainy, mottled texture real mineral pigments like ultramarine or raw umber produce) rather than a smooth flat digital gradient.
4. DRY-BRUSH ACCENTS — a handful of confident dry-brush strokes at leaf edges, where a near-empty brush drags and skips across the paper, adding organic texture without over-describing.
5. SPARING INK — fine ink line accents only at the focal cluster (a vein, a stem joint), never outlining the whole subject; ink used decoratively everywhere is the single fastest way to make a watercolor read as fake.
6. NEGATIVE SPACE IS ACTIVE — the surrounding white paper is a compositional element, not empty background; keep the stem asymmetric and off-center so the white space has shape and rhythm.

Medium/technique: painted wet-on-wet with soft feathered color bleeds and gentle blooms, translucent layered washes (2-3 passes), a few confident dry-brush leaf edges, and fine delicate ink line accents drawn sparingly over the paint.

Visual qualities: visible cold-press watercolor paper texture and fiber grain. Palette: muted sage greens and soft blush pink, dusty warm neutrals, pigment granulating naturally into the paper's tooth, kept to 3-4 pigments total so the color harmony stays coherent rather than muddy.

Background/composition: generous surrounding white space so the subject floats and breathes as active negative space; single off-center stem arcing across the frame per classical botanical-plate convention, asymmetric and airy, roughly a third of the frame occupied by the subject.

Aspect ratio: 4:5 (print/card standard). For a wider card-front layout, 3:2 landscape with the stem arcing horizontally also works from the same brief.

Mood: calm, organic, hand-made, gallery quality. Ultra-detailed focal area, natural imperfect edges, high resolution.

Consistency note: if you're building a matched set (a run of botanical prints or a card line), keep the palette description and paper-texture wording identical across every subject and generate the set from the same fixed seed where your SD UI exposes one — a locked seed plus an unchanged prompt scaffold reliably holds the same paper texture and color harmony across different subjects, a real advantage Stable Diffusion has over prompt-only consistency attempts on Midjourney or gpt-image.

Suggested SDXL settings: 25-35 sampling steps, DPM++ 2M Karras or Euler a sampler, CFG scale 5-7 (watercolor washes degrade into oversaturated hard edges above ~9), native SDXL resolution 1024×1280 for the 4:5 crop.

Negative prompt: digital art, vector, hard edges, bold outlines, 3D render, photorealistic, oversaturated, neon, heavy black, busy background, frame, border, text, watermark, signature

promptText:
Style: an ultra-cute, toy-like isometric miniature diorama — the polished, collectible-toy-line look of a shelf-display piece, with true tilt-shift optics (not just small scale) doing the "miniature" illusion.

Subject: [SUBJECT, e.g. a tiny cozy coffee shop on a street corner], rendered as a collectible toy world with tidy little props (a lamppost, a bench, a potted tree, a striped awning), each modeled with the same rounded-corner radius so the whole set reads as one cohesive toy line rather than mismatched assets.

Technique checklist (the specifics that sell "toy" rather than "small building"):
1. TRUE ISOMETRIC CAMERA — orthographic-feeling 3/4 top-down view, camera angled at roughly 35-45° elevation and 45° azimuth, parallel edges rather than converging perspective lines, the defining trait of an isometric diorama versus a normal 3D render shrunk down.
2. TILT-SHIFT IS OPTICAL, NOT A FILTER — a genuine narrow sharp focal band across the main subject (roughly the middle third of the frame) with soft, increasing optical blur toward the top and bottom edges specifically — this selective-focus falloff is the actual mechanism that tricks the eye into reading scale as tiny.
3. UNIFORM BEVEL LANGUAGE — every object shares the same rounded-corner radius and matte-clay surface finish; mixing sharp-edged and rounded objects in one diorama is the fastest way to break the toy-line cohesion.
4. TWO-TONE SHADING PER OBJECT — a light-side and shadow-side tone per surface rather than one flat fill, giving gentle dimensionality without photoreal texture.
5. LIGHT-SOURCE DISCIPLINE — one warm golden-hour key light from the upper-left casts consistent, proportionally-scaled ambient-occlusion contact shadows under every object; shadow direction and softness must agree across all props.
6. ONE ACCENT COLOR — reserve the single most saturated color for the tiny lit windows/signage glow; everything else stays in the pastel family so the eye has exactly one place to land.

Medium/technique: clean low-poly geometry, soft rounded toy-like edges, chunky friendly proportions. True isometric 3/4 top-down camera, orthographic feel, genuine tilt-shift miniature effect per the checklist above.

Visual qualities: warm golden-hour key light from the upper left (~3000K color temperature), gentle ambient fill, soft ambient-occlusion contact shadows with falloff proportional to object scale, tiny warm window lights inside catching a hint of bloom. Palette: soft pastels with a single cheerful accent color, cohesive and candy-like, matte clay-render surfaces with two-tone shading per object.

Background/composition: floating on a clean [BACKGROUND COLOR, e.g. soft cream, hex approx #F7F1E8] background, centered composition with even negative space on all sides.

Technique checklist (the specifics a real old-master study leans on):
1. UNDERPAINTING LOGIC — an implied warm umber or verdaccio (grey-green) underlayer shows through the thin passages, so shadows read as transparent and glowing rather than opaque black; this is the single biggest difference between a real old-master glaze method and a flat "dark filter."

6. ONE ACCENT COLOR — a single restrained jewel-tone (deep emerald, oxblood, or gold) reserved for exactly one element (a jewel, a ribbon, an embroidery thread) that the eye keeps returning to against the otherwise earth-toned palette.

Luminous flesh tones built in thin warm glazes over the shadow side and thicker, cooler, more opaque paint in the lit flesh, with one crisp soft catchlight in each eye. Palette: raw umber, ivory black, warm ochre, and burnt sienna doing most of the work, with one restrained jewel-tone accent.

promptText:
Style: a clean, modern flat-design vector "spot" illustration in a corporate-editorial style — bold, simplified geometric forms with confident single-weight linework, the polished, design-forward look of a contemporary publication's spot art rather than corporate-stiff clip-art.

Subject: [CONCEPT, e.g. a person working at a laptop surrounded by floating charts, sticky notes, and idea bubbles], reduced to its clearest, most legible silhouette — a viewer should read the concept in under a second.

Technique checklist (the specifics that separate real editorial spot art from generic flat-icon clip-art):
1. SINGLE LINE WEIGHT, USED SPARINGLY — sharp linework of one consistent weight (roughly a 3-4px equivalent at final size), applied only where two same-value shapes meet, never as decorative outline around everything.
2. DEPTH VIA OCCLUSION, NOT GRADIENT — a few deliberate layered overlaps between shapes (the laptop overlapping the desk, a chart overlapping a sticky note) imply depth through what's in front of what, never a soft shadow or gradient fill.
3. GRAIN BREAKS THE FLATNESS — a subtle film-grain or fine halftone-grain overlay at low opacity (roughly 5-8%) prevents the flat color fields from reading as sterile digital vector.
4. 60-30-10 COLOR DISCIPLINE — a dominant color at ~60% of the shape area, a secondary at ~30%, and exactly one bright accent at ~10% reserved for the single focal element, so hierarchy reads instantly without a caption.
5. SCATTERED SCALE ACCENTS — small floating accent shapes (dots, arcs, tick-marks) at varied scale for visual rhythm, never uniform size/spacing which reads as a template pattern rather than illustration.
6. GRID-ALIGNED COMPOSITION — the subject and its negative space sit on an implied grid (think a 12-column editorial layout), so the open space beside the subject looks like a designed column, not leftover margin.

Medium/technique: sharp linework, subtle grain overlay, layered shape overlaps for depth, small floating accent shapes at varied scale.

Visual qualities: a limited, harmonious three-color scheme of teal, coral, and cream (swap to [BRAND COLORS] if provided) built on the 60-30-10 distribution above — no heavy gradients, no more than one tint/shade step per hue.

Background/composition: subject anchored to one side of the frame with deliberate open negative space beside it, grid-aligned, sized for a headline or caption. Plain off-white background, no competing texture.

Aspect ratio: 3:2 (landscape, to sit beside an article or slide). For a square social-card crop, 1:1 with the subject shifted to one third and the accent shapes filling the remaining space works from the same brief.

Mood/quality: friendly, smart, contemporary, editorial rather than corporate-stiff; crisp scalable-vector cleanliness, smooth clean edges, polished digital-illustration finish.

Consistency note: a spot illustration like this is rarely a one-off — a publication typically needs a whole family of them across articles, all reading as one visual system. This is exactly the limitation OpenAI documents for gpt-image/DALL·E: it does not reliably reproduce identical shapes, colors, or characters across separate generations of the same prompt. Style: a cinematic anime illustration blending Niji-model line/detail work with moody, two-color cyberpunk lighting — classic forced-perspective staging that exaggerates scale and atmosphere over literal realism, in the tradition of Blade Runner-influenced anime cityscapes.

Subject: [A LONE CHARACTER, e.g. a hooded courier] standing in a narrow rain-soaked neon alley at night, reading as small and a little lonely against the environment's scale rather than heroic.

Technique checklist (what makes this read as genuine cinematic cyberpunk rather than a generic neon-city render):
1. LOW FORCED-PERSPECTIVE CAMERA — a low dramatic angle (roughly 24mm-wide-angle-equivalent field of view) that exaggerates the height of the walls closing in overhead; this single choice does more for atmosphere than any amount of extra signage.
2. TWO-COLOR LIGHTING, NOT A RAINBOW — saturated magenta key light from one side of the alley answered by cyan/teal from the other (~2 competing color temperatures, no third competing hue except the one warm accent below); mixing in a third saturated color flattens the mood instead of deepening it.
3. RIM LIGHT SEPARATES THE SUBJECT — a strong rim light traces the character's silhouette against the dark background so they don't visually merge into the alley clutter.
4. LIGHT OBEYS ITS SOURCE — bloom and lens flare concentrate only at real sign edges and practical lights, never scattered decoratively across the frame.
5. WET SURFACES DOUBLE EVERYTHING BELOW THE HORIZON — every light source has a rippling, slightly-broken specular reflection in the puddled pavement; a dry-looking street breaks the whole illusion.
6. DEPTH THROUGH LAYERED FOCUS — sharp signage and detail in the near-foreground, progressively softer and hazier signage in the mid and background, thick atmospheric haze compressing the far background into soft color blocks — real depth-of-field falloff, not uniform sharpness front-to-back.
7. ONE WARM ACCENT — a single warm light (a distant sodium streetlamp or a lit noodle-stall sign) breaks the cool magenta/cyan duo so the palette doesn't read as monotone.

Medium/technique: towering walls plastered with glowing holographic signage and flickering kanji at varied depths, tangled cable bundles and paper lanterns strung overhead, steam venting from a grate mid-frame, hyper-detailed signage typography and grime. Individual rain streaks catch light as they fall; puddle ripples show soft specular breakup.

Visual qualities: color temperature roughly 8000-10000K equivalent on the cyan side against a warm ~2700K accent point, high local contrast between glowing signage and ink-black shadow. Palette: saturated magenta and cyan/electric-blue as the dominant duo against a deep near-black base, with the single warm accent per the checklist above.

Background/composition: strong one-point perspective driving straight down the alley toward a glowing vanishing point, the character placed at the lower third as the clear, unambiguous focal point against the visual noise around them.

Aspect ratio: 16:9. For a taller poster crop that emphasizes the towering walls even more, 2:3 vertical also works from the same brief with the vanishing point pushed higher in frame.

Negative / avoid: flat even lighting, a third competing saturated hue, dry unreflective pavement, cluttered signage with no depth layering, washed-out low-contrast haze, daylight, text/watermark/signature.

Consistency note: for a multi-panel cyberpunk set (e.g. establishing shot + close-up of the same character), keep the character description, coat/hood silhouette, and the magenta/cyan lighting wording identical across prompts, and generate them back-to-back in the same session — Midjourney's --niji model does not guarantee an identical character across separate independent generations.

promptText:
Role/Reference: Shoot this as a strobe-frozen advertising still, the technique studios use for method, Aesop, and craft-food campaigns when they want the product to look like it just erupted mid-air. The physical basis is real: a mono-light or speedlight fired at high-speed-sync (or a dedicated flash-duration strobe at t.1 ≈ 1/8000s) freezes fast-falling and tossed elements with zero motion blur — that flash-duration ceiling is what this whole composition depends on, so treat "frozen at strobe-speed peak" as a hard technical constraint, not a mood word.

Resolution/Format: High-resolution advertising macro photograph, portrait orientation, aspect ratio 4:5 (Midjourney: --ar 4:5 --v 6.1 --stylize 250 --chaos 5 — low stylize keeps the geometry photographically literal rather than illustrative; a little chaos gives natural variation to ingredient scatter without breaking the arrangement logic).

Product: A [BAR OF SOAP / PROTEIN SCOOP] as the hero, with its key ingredients — [FRESH MINT LEAVES, CITRUS SLICES, COCOA BEANS] — captured at the exact peak of a levitation shot: each element frozen at a distinct point in its own arc (some still rising, some at apex, some just starting to fall) so the cluster reads as one continuous captured moment rather than a static pile. Stagger distance-from-lens deliberately — nearest ingredient roughly 15-20cm from the product, furthest 35-40cm+ — with size and focus falloff scaled to that real depth, so the arrangement reads three-dimensional and orbital rather than a flat pasted collage.

Surface/Background: A soft, seamless [pastel] gradient sweep (paper or fabric, lit as a true backdrop, not a flat color fill), exposed one to one-and-a-half stops brighter at the top of frame than at the base to keep the sweep looking genuinely lit rather than a digital gradient. Reserve clean, unbroken negative space in the upper third for a headline.

Lighting: A large softbox or beauty dish as key, positioned high and slightly off-axis (35-45°) for a broad, even wraparound light with a soft-edged falloff; a white bounce or a low-power fill flash camera-left holds the shadow side open at roughly a 2:1 ratio — bright enough to read every ingredient's texture, restrained enough to keep one clear falloff direction. One single, soft contact shadow directly beneath the product on the sweep is the visual anchor that keeps a floating composition from looking unmoored; no secondary shadows from the orbiting ingredients should compete with it.

Camera/Angle: As though on a 100mm macro lens at f/8-f/11 — the aperture band that holds both the product and its nearest orbiting ingredients acceptably sharp via depth of field while the furthest ingredients fall into gentle real optical blur (not digital blur), and stays a stop or two clear of diffraction softening past f/16. Eye-level to the product, camera locked off, no perspective distortion.

Focus/Material detail: Every ingredient rendered hyper-detailed at true macro scale — mint's leaf venation and surface fuzz, citrus's pith fiber and glistening juice-sheen, cocoa's rough matte husk grain — genuine material differences between elements, never a uniform waxy render. Product surface (soap's edge bevel and lather sheen, or the scoop's brushed/matte plastic) equally crisp, label or embossing intended to be legible. Note: exact readable label/embossed text is a documented weak spot for image models (flagged directly in OpenAI's gpt-image/DALL·E guidance), so if the copy must be real, check it at full crop and plan a regenerate-or-retouch pass. Grade vibrant but natural, punchy without highlight clipping.

Avoid (--no): motion blur, ingredients that look glued or randomly scattered rather than orbiting with intent, multiple competing shadow directions, blown highlights, warped or duplicated label text, cluttered backdrop, watermark, extra logos.

promptText:
Role/Reference: Light and stage this exactly the way a packaging-photography studio preps a mockup for a client pitch before the final brand mark exists — a genuine studio set (softbox, bounce, seamless or textured surface) rather than a rendered 3D box on a gradient, which is the single biggest tell separating a convincing mockup from an obvious CGI comp.

Resolution/Format: High-resolution photoreal packaging photograph, portrait orientation, aspect ratio 4:5 (Midjourney: --ar 4:5 --v 6.1 --stylize 150 — kept low because photoreal packaging needs literal material rendering, not painterly interpretation).

Product: [A MATTE KRAFT COSMETIC BOX AND TUBE] standing together, staged as a genuine studio product photo. Reserve one clean panel on the box's front face as a deboss-only logo placeholder: a shallow recessed impression (roughly 0.3-0.5mm equivalent depth) with a soft, physically-consistent self-shadow tracing its inner edge — built the way a real deboss die would press it, catching light on one side and casting a matching micro-shadow on the other — left entirely blank so a logo can later be composited into that exact shadow geometry without re-lighting.

Surface/Background: A smooth, neutral [plaster] surface, camera-matched in tone so it doesn't compete with the kraft paper's warm hue. Depth of field (as though 90mm macro at f/8) keeps both packaging pieces sharp while the plaster background softens gently toward the frame edges — real optical falloff, not a background blur filter. Centered composition, even breathing room on all sides.

Lighting: A large diffusion source (equivalent to a 3x4ft softbox) as key from camera-right, positioned several feet back for a long, soft-edged shadow rather than a hard-edged one — matte kraft and soft-touch coatings have no specular sheen to speak of, so hard light only reveals surface flaws. A white v-flat or bounce card camera-left lifts the shadow side by roughly one stop, avoiding a flat, contrast-free look while still keeping shadow edges soft. Contact shadows beneath both pieces should read as soft, believable, and grounded — no floating packaging.

Camera/Angle: As though on a 90mm macro lens at f/8, three-quarter-front hero angle, enough depth of field to hold both pieces sharp against the softened background.

Focus/Material detail: Materials render with true surface behavior — visible kraft paper grain and subtle fiber texture, soft-touch coating reading as a low, broad sheen (never gloss), crisp die-cut edges with no fraying or warping. Camera/retouch to e-commerce branding-photography finish: ultra-clean, no dust, no fingerprints. Note for the next pass: once a real logo is composited or generated into the blank deboss panel, treat that as its own iterative step — exact, crisp, readable logo/text rendering (especially matching debossed shadow geometry) is a documented weak spot for image models, most explicitly flagged in OpenAI's gpt-image/DALL·E guidance — expect two or three regenerate/retouch passes before the shadow geometry and the letterforms agree.

Avoid (--no): any existing logo, text, or artwork appearing on the blank debossed panel, warped or distorted packaging geometry, harsh directional shadows, clutter, competing brand marks, dust, fingerprints, watermark.

promptText:
Role/Reference: Shoot this the way a merchandising or editorial flat-lay photographer rigs an overhead set — camera on a horizontal boom or copy stand directly above the surface, dead-parallel to it, so there is zero lens-induced perspective convergence across the grid. That parallel rig is what makes a flat lay read as "designed" rather than "photographed from an angle and corrected in post."

Resolution/Format: High-resolution top-down merchandising flat-lay photograph, square format, aspect ratio 1:1 (Midjourney: --ar 1:1 --v 6.1 --stylize 200).

Product: [FIVE LIPSTICK TUBES / A SKINCARE SET] arranged in a precise, evenly-spaced grid — gaps measured to a consistent module (think a stylist's ruler-straight grid: equal gutters both horizontally and vertically, items aligned to invisible grid lines, not eyeballed) so the repetition itself becomes the visual interest rather than the individual products competing for attention. Tuck complementary props — [dried flowers, a length of ribbon, painted color swatches] — into the grid's negative space between items, sized and placed so they add life without breaking the grid's rhythm or overlapping any product's silhouette.

Surface/Background: On [textured handmade paper]. A disciplined [warm terracotta and cream] palette carried through paper, props, and packaging alike — the restraint of a single controlled palette is what reads as "curated merchandising" rather than "random objects on a table." Reserve deliberate, undecorated negative space (consistent paper tone, zero prop bleed) sized and positioned for a title or logo lockup.

Lighting: Camera dead-overhead and parallel to the surface (a boom arm or copy-stand rig, not a handheld angle correctable in post). One large, soft overhead source — a broad diffusion panel offset a few degrees off-vertical so the light has direction rather than reading dead-flat and shadowless — producing gentle, evenly diffused shadows with soft edges and one consistent direction across every single item. No competing shadow directions between products: that's the fastest tell of a flat lay lit by multiple uncoordinated sources rather than one considered rig.

Camera/Angle: As though on a 50mm lens at f/8-f/11 — the aperture band that holds genuinely even edge-to-edge sharpness across a flat plane with no perspective distortion at any point in the grid, unlike a wider lens which would need correcting.

Focus/Material detail: Every product label crisp and fully legible at 100% crop — a true parallel overhead rig needs no perspective correction, so there's no excuse for a soft or skewed label. Note: exact, readable label copy across a whole grid of packaging is a harder ask than a single hero shot and is a documented weak spot for image models generally (OpenAI's gpt-image/DALL·E guidance flags this explicitly); check every item's label at full crop and plan to regenerate or retouch the ones that garble. True material micro-texture on each item — lipstick tube metal or matte finish, cream jar glass, paper's handmade fiber grain.

Avoid (--no): crooked or unevenly spaced items, any camera tilt or perspective convergence, visual clutter, clashing colors, harsh or multi-directional shadows, competing brand logos, added text, watermark.

Fill in the product and background-tone brackets; keep --ar 4:5 for premium/luxury ad crops
promptText:
Role/Reference: Light this the way a luxury-campaign photographer lights a hero product for print — Chanel No.5, Hennessy, and high-end watch campaigns share the same underlying discipline: one hard, undiffused source and nothing else. The mystery comes from what the light refuses to reveal, not from a dimmed version of even studio lighting, so single-source discipline is the entire technical premise here.

Resolution/Format: High-resolution dramatic low-key advertising photograph, portrait orientation, aspect ratio 4:5 (Midjourney: --ar 4:5 --v 6.1 --stylize 300 — higher stylize suits the graphic, high-contrast nature of low-key work).

Product: A [CRYSTAL WHISKY BOTTLE / LUXURY WATCH], one hero product, sculpted by a single hard, undiffused spotlight or snooted/gridded strobe as the only key — positioned at a steep 60-75° raking angle so it carves strong, defined highlights across the form while the rest falls to fast, near-black shadow. No fill light of any kind: the falloff to black is the effect, and adding fill would collapse the entire premise (equivalent to a lighting ratio well beyond 8:1).

Surface/Background: A dark, moody [charcoal] gradient, graded to recede to near-black at the frame edges, with faint, sparse smoke wisps drifting through the negative space — motivated as if a haze machine sat just off-camera, giving the hard key beam visible volume the way stage and campaign lighting uses haze to make a light source "visible" in the air, not just on the subject. The surface beneath the product is wet and glass-reflective, throwing a controlled, slightly softened mirror reflection that grounds the product without competing with it. Leave dark, low-detail negative space for an elegant headline to sit directly on the near-black background.

Lighting: The single hard key described above is the only light source — confirm every specular highlight in the frame traces back to that one source's actual position; no secondary highlight should appear on a facet or surface that source geometrically couldn't reach, since an "impossible highlight" is the fastest tell of a lighting setup that wasn't actually reasoned through.

Camera/Angle: As though on a Hasselblad medium-format body, 80mm lens at f/2.8 — enough shallow depth of field to let any background smoke soften into atmosphere while the entire product plane stays critically sharp.

Focus/Material detail: Materials read genuinely luxurious — [cut crystal facets throwing small, crisp internal highlights and refracted light shards / polished metal with narrow, hard-edged specular lines following the case's curvature]. Label or dial face stays fully legible only where the key light directly strikes it, with unlit areas falling into rich, detail-retained near-black rather than a crushed featureless void — real low-key work protects a sliver of shadow detail even at its darkest. Note: exact, readable label or dial-face text/numerals under this kind of hard, partial lighting is a documented weak spot for image models (flagged explicitly in OpenAI's gpt-image/DALL·E guidance) — check that detail closely and plan to regenerate or retouch if it must carry real copy. Retouch to sophisticated luxury-campaign finish: deep, rich blacks with retained micro-contrast, never muddy grey shadows.

Avoid (--no): flat or evenly lit product (defeats the entire low-key premise), blown highlights, fully crushed featureless blacks, clutter, distracting secondary reflections, warped label or dial, added text, watermark.

name: Minimal Luxury Monogram
summary: An elegant intertwined-initials mark with refined linework for a premium or fashion brand.
description: An elegant intertwined-initials mark with refined linework for a premium or fashion brand.
whatYouGet: A monogram built in Subject → Construction geometry → Color/style → Background/negative-space → Aspect-ratio order: two initials merged via genuine shared-stroke ligature construction, not simply overlapped

A single thin, constant line weight (calibrated to survive foil-stamping/engraving) with the overlap counterform treated as deliberately shaped negative space, in a restrained matte-black-on-cream palette (swappable)

An honest note on letterform reliability built into the prompt itself — because this is custom lettering rather than a symbol, it flags Ideogram or Google Gemini/Imagen as a stronger legibility check than Midjourney/gpt-image

Swap the "[AB]" initials and [matte black on warm cream] palette; run the same brief through Ideogram or Google Gemini/Imagen as a legibility check on the exact stroke overlap, then hand-refine in a vector editor for a production-ready mark
promptText:
Role/Reference: Approach this the way a type-literate identity designer builds a ligature monogram for a heritage or luxury house — in the register of Cartier's interlocking-C or YSL's stacked mark — where the two letters are engineered from a shared construction system, never simply overlapped.

Subject: a luxury monogram for the initials "[AB]" — not two letters placed side by side, but one new glyph derived from where the strokes of [A] and [B] can legitimately share a stem, bowl, or crossbar without either letter losing legibility.

Construction geometry: build both letters from the same geometric letterform family — matching x-height, matching curve radii (construct any bowls from the same circle-and-tangent-line logic classic geometric monograms use, so curves feel drawn with a single compass setting), matching terminal angles — so the two letters read as one coherent mark rather than two typefaces forced together. Apply the same optical corrections a type designer would: where the merged stroke crosses a curve, thicken it fractionally (1-2%) so it doesn't read as visually thinner at the overlap, the way real logotype construction compensates for the eye's tendency to see intersections as lighter. Hold the linework to a single thin weight throughout — thin enough to feel refined, thick enough to survive foil-stamping or engraving at 10mm — with zero weight variation between the two letters, held to strict bilateral or rotational symmetry.

Color and style: a restrained matte-black-on-cream palette (swappable), zero gradient, texture, or tonal shading — restraint here is the actual luxury signal, not applied ornament; a heritage mark earns its authority by having nothing to hide behind.

Background and negative space: center the mark on a warm off-white background rather than pure white — warm cream signals tactility (paper stock, wax seal, woven fabric), the register true luxury and hospitality marks live in versus bright digital white — with generous clear-space equal to roughly one letterform's width on all sides. Treat the negative space carved at the overlap as the mark's most important real estate: the counterform where the letters cross should be a clean, deliberate shape in its own right, not an accidental gap.

Aspect ratio and format: square, delivered as an isolated mark only. --ar 1:1 --v 6.1 --style raw --no serif flourishes beyond what the letterforms themselves require, extra ornament, crest, frame, photorealism, shadow, mockup, wordmark, tagline.

Text-rendering reality check: even at just two characters, this is a letterform-construction exercise, not free illustration — Midjourney (and OpenAI's gpt-image/DALL-E, if used instead) can still distort a stroke, thicken one side unevenly, or subtly misshape a letterform under the pressure of merging two glyphs into one. Generate several variations and pick the cleanest, or run the same brief through Ideogram or Google's Gemini/Imagen — both generally more reliable for precise in-image lettering — as a legibility check before treating any monogram as final. For production use, hand-trace the chosen output in a vector editor (Illustrator/Figma) rather than shipping the raster render directly.

name: Geometric Tech Wordmark

description: A crisp, perfectly kerned wordmark with a modern electric gradient for a tech startup.
whatYouGet: Your exact brand name built in Subject → Construction geometry → Color/style → Background/negative-space → Aspect-ratio order: a true rounded-geometric-sans letterform family (Poppins/Futura/Circular-style circular counters, near-zero stroke contrast, rounded terminals) on plain white

Optically corrected kerning on the pairs that always look loose by default (AV, AW, LT, TA) and tightened spacing on round-letter collisions (OO, CO), with every glyph locked to one shared baseline and cap-height

An analogous, even-luminance horizontal gradient (electric-blue to cyan by default, swappable), plus a built-in honest caveat pointing to Gemini/Imagen or Ideogram over gpt-image/Midjourney for the exact-text pass, per OpenAI's own documented text-rendering limitations

Fill in "[BRAND NAME]" and the two gradient colors; check spelling and baseline alignment letter-by-letter in the output regardless of model — if you started in Midjourney or gpt-image for style exploration, re-run the final version through Gemini/Imagen or Ideogram before shipping
promptText:
Role/Reference: Build this the way a type-focused brand studio finalizes a tech wordmark for production — the same optical-kerning discipline used on marks like Circular- or Poppins-based startup logotypes, where every pair of letters is individually adjusted rather than left at a typeface's default metrics.

Subject: a wordmark logo rendering the exact text "[BRAND NAME]" in a rounded geometric sans-serif — the same letterform family as Poppins, Futura, or Circular: true circles for the counters of O/C/G, consistent near-zero stroke contrast, and rounded terminals rather than sharp cut ends, the specific typographic signal for "modern tech" versus a grotesque sans reading corporate or a humanist sans reading friendly-SaaS. Wordmark only, no icon or symbol alongside it.

Construction geometry: kern optically, not mechanically. Tighten the pairs that always look loose at default metrics — AV, AW, LT, TA, VA typically need 5-8% of the em tightened — and open up pairs prone to visual collision, especially round-into-round letters like OO or CO, which need a touch more space than their bounding boxes suggest or they read as merging. Hold overall tracking slightly open, roughly +10 to +20 units, so the name doesn't feel cramped at small header sizes. Align every glyph to a shared baseline and identical cap-height — no letter should sit even a pixel off that line, since baseline drift (a curved letter appearing to "float" a hair above its neighbors) is one of the fastest tells of an AI-generated wordmark versus a properly type-set one.

Color and style: fill the letters with a smooth horizontal gradient from [electric-blue] (left) to [cyan] (right) — this cool-to-cool, analogous direction, roughly 20-40° apart on the color wheel, reads as trust plus energy without the jarring visual snap a complementary (opposite-hue) gradient would introduce. Keep the gradient's luminance roughly even across its length — if one end of the ramp gets meaningfully darker than the other, that end's letters read as harder to see, undermining the wordmark's legibility at a glance.

Background and negative space: set on pure white with generous side clear-space equal to the cap-height on both left and right.

Aspect ratio and format: wide (3:1), high resolution, crisp anti-aliased edges, zero gradient banding. --ar 3:1 --no icon, symbol, tagline, shadow, outline, 3D, background shapes, misspelling, dropped or duplicated characters.

Text-rendering reality check: spell the brand name exactly as written and verify it letter-by-letter in the output — text rendering, especially inside a gradient fill, is still the one place image models fail silently. Per OpenAI's own documentation, gpt-image/DALL-E "can still struggle with precise text placement and clarity" and with keeping recurring brand elements consistent across regenerations; Midjourney needs the same extra scrutiny. Google's Gemini/Imagen (Nano Banana) or Ideogram are generally the stronger choices whenever exact wordmark text must render cleanly — use one of those for the final text-legible pass even if another tool was used for early style exploration, and re-check kerning and baseline alignment glyph-by-glyph before shipping.

Fill in the brand type, central icon, "[BRAND NAME]", "[EST. 2024]" and the two-tone palette; check that both curved arcs match the ring radius and that spelling is exact in whichever model produces the final legible version
promptText:
Role/Reference: Construct this the way classic Americana badge design actually works — Pendleton labels, old apothecary seals, National Park Service emblems — all built on a genuine two-ring construction system with curved type set to follow the ring's own radius, the same way a vector artist uses "type on a path" with a precisely matched path radius rather than eyeballing a curve.

Subject: a vintage circular emblem badge for [a coffee roastery / craft brand], centered on a single confident line-art illustration of [a coffee bean / mountain / anchor] in the innermost field.

Construction geometry: start from the ring system — two concentric rings with a consistent gap between them, wide enough to hold curved type comfortably without crowding the inner illustration (a gap roughly 12-15% of the badge's overall radius is a reliable ratio) — and set every curved baseline to match that ring's radius exactly. Text following a tighter or looser arc than the ring it sits inside is the single most common tell of a badge that wasn't actually constructed on a circle, versus type dropped onto an arc as an afterthought. Render the central illustration with consistent stroke weight throughout, and hold the whole composition to strict rotational symmetry around the vertical axis. Establish clear three-tier hierarchy: the curved brand name along the top inner arc (largest, boldest weight), the curved establishment date along the bottom inner arc (smaller, more letter-spaced so it doesn't visually compete with the name), and small star or dot separators placed exactly where the two arcs meet, left and right — sized to balance the visual gap rather than filling it arbitrarily.

Color and style: a two-tone palette only — [cream on deep brown] — badge design has always been two-tone by necessity (screen printing, embroidery, and stamping all favor it), and that production constraint is what gives the style its authenticity rather than a look that merely references vintage from a distance. Crisp, tidy edges: a clean flat-vector reproduction of the heritage style, not a distressed or grunge-textured pastiche of it.

Background and negative space: isolated badge on a plain white background, with the central illustration given enough negative space that it doesn't crowd the ring border.

Aspect ratio and format: square. --ar 1:1 --style raw --v 6.1 --no photorealism, distressed texture, grunge, clutter, mockup, gradient, drop shadow.

Text-rendering reality check: the curved brand name "[BRAND NAME]" along the top arc and "[EST. 2024]" along the bottom arc must render as clean, bold, legible curved type matched exactly to the ring's radius, spelled exactly as written. Curved, arc-fitted lettering is a harder case for every current image model — Midjourney and OpenAI's gpt-image/DALL-E are both prone to distorted, unevenly spaced, or misaligned-to-radius text once it's bent to a curve — so treat Midjourney's output as a construction/geometry draft only, and run the final curved-text pass through Ideogram or Google Gemini/Imagen, both notably more reliable for in-image lettering, before treating the badge as finished. For production, re-set the final wordmark on an actual vector path at the ring's true radius rather than shipping the raster output directly.

promptText:
Role/Reference: Draw this the way a genuine single-line artist works — in the tradition of Picasso's one-line animal sketches or modern continuous-line illustration — where the entire form is planned in advance as one unbroken path (an Euler path: every point reachable without lifting the pen and without retracing a segment), not merely a shape that happens to look line-like after the fact.

promptText:
Work to the standard of a senior product-icon designer at an Apple/Google-caliber studio, where an app icon is judged the same way a wordmark is: does it survive being shrunk to a 40px dot among fifty other icons on a stranger's home screen. This is a glanceability exercise, not a boutique illustration.

Subject: a mobile app icon in a rounded-square (squircle) format for [APP NAME], centered on one simple glyph — [lightning bolt / leaf / chat bubble] — reduced to its most minimal recognizable form. Pick the single silhouette that reads a genre (communication, growth, energy, etc.) in under a quarter second; anything requiring a second look at 1024px will fail completely at 40px.

Construction geometry: build the tile as a true superellipse, not a rounded-rectangle approximation — mathematically |x/a|^n + |y/b|^n = 1 with an exponent n in the 4–5 range, which is the same family of curve Apple's own icon grid specifies. The visual tell of a real superellipse versus a cheap corner-radius fake is that the curve's rate of change is continuous all the way around; a rounded-rectangle has a visible seam where the straight edge meets the arc, a superellipse doesn't. Commit the glyph fully to one stylistic system — either a consistent-weight line (stroke roughly 8–10% of the glyph's height, held uniform through every curve and terminal) or a clean solid silhouette — never mixed within the same mark. Center the glyph to its *optical* center, not its geometric bounding-box center: a glyph with more visual weight toward the bottom (like a filled chat bubble's tail) needs to sit fractionally higher than dead-center to read as balanced, the same optical-correction trick type designers use when centering glyphs in a cap-height box. Hold the glyph to 55–60% of the tile's width so there's breathing room on all sides — packed-tight icons lose legibility against a busy wallpaper, oversized-empty ones look unfinished.

Color and style: a bright solid [golden-yellow] tile paired with [black] for the glyph. Yellow at full saturation sits at the top of the perceived-luminance curve of any hue, which is precisely the physiological reason it's used for hazard signage and why it's the right call here — the brief is "gets noticed in a grid," not "feels premium and quiet." Yellow-on-black is also one of the highest-contrast pairings available (informally in the high-teens on a WCAG-style contrast-ratio scale) and stays legible for red-green colorblind users, unlike a red/green or red/orange pairing. Render flat, no gradient banding, crisp anti-aliased vector edges — gradients introduce banding artifacts at small export sizes and cost contrast for no legibility gain.

Background and negative space: the solid tile IS the whole background — no separate backdrop, frame, drop shadow, or device mockup. Deliver the raw square un-masked; the OS applies its own corner mask and shadow at render time, so a pre-rounded or pre-shadowed export just gets double-processed and looks off. Mentally check legibility at 40px before finalizing — the 1024px canvas is production spec, not the real reading distance.

Aspect ratio and format: square, 1024×1024, no alpha-transparency tricks, full-bleed color to every edge. --ar 1:1 --v 6.1 --stylize 50 (low stylize keeps Midjourney from over-embellishing a mark that needs to stay simple) --no gradient banding, text, letters, numbers, photorealism, outer border, busy detail, drop shadow, bevel, 3D render. This is the exact correction professional type and icon designers apply and it is the single biggest tell between an amateur set and a real one. Hold one constant 2px stroke weight (roughly 8% of the 24px cell height) across all sixteen, one consistent corner-radius on every rounded terminal, and one consistent cap/join style — rounded caps and joins throughout, never mixed with square or mitered ones. Design this to the construction principles a professional character-design studio uses for edutainment mascots — the lineage that runs from classic animation model sheets through Duolingo's owl and Khan Academy's Kes — where the shape has to work as a piece of graphic design first and a character second.

Subject: a flat-vector mascot of [a smiling fox / robot] for [a kids learning app], front-facing, in a confident, grounded stance — base or feet planted wider than the torso, weight low, nothing balanced precariously — since a stable silhouette reads as approachable and a top-heavy or off-balance one reads as unsettling to a young audience without them being able to say why.

This shapes-first discipline is the same one used in classic model-sheet character design and it's what stops a mascot from collapsing into noise at small sizes. Hold outline weight perfectly uniform across the whole figure — a stroke that thickens or thins as it travels around a curve is the single most common amateur tell in vector character work, since professional vector tools hold constant stroke width by construction, not by eye. Reduce the face to the minimum marks that convey warmth: simply-shaped eyes and one confident curved smile line, nothing more. Set the eyes larger than natural proportion and below the head's vertical midpoint — this is the "baby schema" (kindchenschema) proportion set identified by ethologist Konrad Lorenz and used across the genre from Pixar to Sesame Street specifically because oversized, low-set eyes trigger an innate caretaking/warmth response in viewers, which is exactly the read a kids' app mascot needs.

Color and style: a near-complementary [orange and teal] palette — orange sits around 30° and teal around 180° on the color wheel, roughly opposite each other, which is what gives the pairing its perceptual energy and its clean differentiation between the character's main shapes. That differentiation matters specifically for an audience still building color-recognition skills, where muddy or low-contrast adjacent colors (e.g. two different greens) are harder to tell apart. Add exactly one soft accent color at 10% coverage or less for a single distinguishing detail (a belly patch, a bandana) — more than one accent starts competing with the primary palette. Render in flat solid fills only, no gradients or cel-shading — flat color blocks hold their read at the small sizes a mobile app renders a mascot avatar or loading animation at, where gradients degrade into muddy noise.

Background and negative space: center the character on plain white with even margins on all sides, nothing behind it competing for attention.

Aspect ratio and format: square. --ar 1:1 --v 6.1 --no text, logotype, photorealism, drop shadow, busy detail, extra props, inconsistent outline weights, eyes above the head's vertical midpoint, mixed shading styles. whatYouGet: Tight 16:9 face-forward crop from just above the head to the upper chest — deliberately tighter than a normal portrait, since crop distance is the single biggest lever for emotional legibility at thumbnail scale
Your uploaded photo pushed to an exaggerated excited/stunned/thrilled reaction while identity and bone structure stay fully locked, with tack-sharp focus locked on the eyes
Bold color-gradient background on the right third with a subtle glow, leaving deliberate, generous negative space on the left sized for a short, oversized headline in a clean bold sans-serif

promptText:
SUBJECT / FOCAL POINT: The uploaded photo is the fixed reference for face, bone structure, and likeness — unmistakably the same person, features and skin untouched, no beautifying pass. Push only the expression, to an exaggerated [excited / stunned / thrilled] reaction. Thumbnail-scale expressions need to resolve in a fraction of a second at a fraction of real size, which is why understated, true-to-life reactions consistently get lost — the exaggeration compensates for the loss of detail, not for a lack of subtlety in the subject.

COMPOSITION: Crop distance on a face is the single highest-leverage variable in thumbnail design — more impactful than background choice or color grade — because the tighter the crop, the fewer pixels the emotion has to travel through to register, which is why the tightest professional thumbnails go noticeably tighter than a comfortable portrait crop would ever go. Crop from just above the head to the upper chest — no headroom to spare, the face IS the composition, not a subject within it. Camera: 85mm-equivalent portrait perspective — long enough to compress facial features flatteringly and avoid the nose-forward distortion a wide lens introduces at close range, the same reason portrait photographers default to 85–135mm rather than 24–35mm for a close-up. Tack-sharp focus locked on the eyes with a visible catchlight, since the eyes need to register as the single sharpest, brightest point in the frame even with the rest of the composition pushed hard for energy. Position the person on the right third against the background, per the rule-of-thirds placement that leaves the left field open.

LIGHTING & COLOR CONTRAST: Dramatic studio key light with a strong rim/hair light for clean edge separation from the background — the classic 3-point-lighting skeleton (key, rim, and a soft fill to keep shadow falloff controlled rather than muddy), vibrant true-to-life skin tones, deliberate shadow falloff for dimension rather than flat, shadowless lighting that reads as artificial. Bold [COLOR] gradient background with a subtle glow behind the subject.

TYPOGRAPHY / TEXT: No text is rendered in this image. Leave deliberate, generous negative space on the left, sized for large headline text — short words, oversized point size, since large simple type is the only typographic choice that survives the resize to thumbnail scale intact. Add that headline afterward in a clean, bold sans-serif for maximum legibility at small sizes.

BACKGROUND: Bold [COLOR] gradient, kept simple and uncluttered so it doesn't compete with the face or the reserved headline space.

ASPECT RATIO: 16:9, face-forward YouTube thumbnail. High-contrast, high-saturation, energetic, photorealistic, ultra sharp, high micro-detail in skin texture and the eyes, 4k. Needs an image-reference model that accepts a photo upload — Nano Banana / Gemini image, or Midjourney with an image prompt, ideally at a high image-weight so identity holds through the expression push — since it edits an existing face; keep the output explicitly at --ar 16:9.

name: Editorial Quote Card
summary: An Instagram-ready 1:1 quote card with clean typographic hierarchy, your handle, and a single tasteful accent shape.
description: An Instagram-ready 1:1 quote card with clean typographic hierarchy, your handle, and a single tasteful accent shape.
whatYouGet: Square 1:1 (1080x1080) Instagram card with your actual quote set as large, centered, bold serif type — line breaks balanced by hand so no line ends on an orphaned word, line-height tuned for calm readability
Your @handle set beneath it in a meaningfully smaller, wide-tracked sans-serif, creating a deliberate size/weight contrast that reads as hierarchy, not decoration
Warm minimal background with exactly one accent geometric shape tucked into a single corner, with generous margins so the type block reads as intentional, floating negative space
install: Since it renders real words, use a model genuinely strong at typography — gpt-image or Ideogram are the safest bets for longer or multi-line quotes; Nano Banana can work with iteration, but classic Midjourney is the weakest of the major tools at legible text and tends to garble longer quotes

Fill in [YOUR QUOTE GOES HERE], [@YOURHANDLE], [BACKGROUND COLOR], and [ACCENT COLOR]; keep the output at 1:1 explicitly. promptText:
Treat this with the same rigor a print editorial spread gets from its art director — type choice, hierarchy, and margin are the entire product here, not decoration around a photo.

SUBJECT / FOCAL POINT: Set '[YOUR QUOTE GOES HERE]' as the unmistakable focal point in a bold modern serif — a serif carries more editorial authority at a glance than a geometric sans, which is exactly why long-form print and premium quote graphics default to one, and it's the fastest way to signal "considered" rather than "templated."

COMPOSITION: At Instagram's feed and grid scale, type hierarchy has to resolve in under a second on a roughly 3-inch phone screen — one dominant size for the words that matter, one clearly smaller size for attribution, and generous line-height so the block reads as calm rather than cramped. Center the quote, size it large, and balance the line breaks by hand rather than letting auto-wrap decide — no line should end on an orphaned one- or two-letter word, the same manual-break discipline a print typesetter applies. Place '[@YOURHANDLE]' beneath the quote, meaningfully smaller and wider-tracked; the size and letterspacing contrast against the serif headline is what manufactures hierarchy, so it needs to read distinctly second, not competing for the same glance. Set comfortable line-height on the quote — roughly 1.3–1.4× the type size, the same range a print body-text spec would call for at this point size — so the block holds together as one calm shape rather than a stack of tight lines. Generous margins on all four sides so the whole text block feels like it's floating centered in the canvas, never edge-to-edge, and note that Instagram crops a slightly tighter square in the profile-grid view than the full 1:1 in-feed view — keep the quote block centered enough to survive that crop.

LIGHTING & COLOR CONTRAST: Warm minimal [BACKGROUND COLOR, e.g. cream] canvas with exactly one subtle [ACCENT COLOR, e.g. terracotta] geometric accent shape tucked into a single corner — one accent shape reads as intentional art direction, a second one starts reading as clutter competing with the type. Refined, premium, calm mood throughout — no visual noise fighting the quote for attention.

TYPOGRAPHY / TEXT: This card lives or dies on its real rendered words, so tool choice matters more here than composition does. The quote: bold modern serif, large, centered, line-height in the 1.3–1.4× range. The handle: clean, wide-tracked sans-serif, meaningfully smaller. Because the quote and handle ARE the deliverable, favor a model genuinely strong at typography — gpt-image or Ideogram are the safest choices for anything longer than a short one-liner, since both have materially stronger text-rendering fidelity than the alternatives; even gpt-image's own guidance flags that precise placement and clarity can still need a second pass, so treat the first render as a draft. Nano Banana can work with iteration. Classic Midjourney is historically the weakest of the major tools at rendering legible text and tends to garble anything past a short phrase — avoid it here, or budget for several regenerations. Whichever tool renders it, check every letter before posting — misspelled type is the one error that's unforgivable on a text-first graphic.

BACKGROUND: Warm minimal [BACKGROUND COLOR] canvas with exactly one accent geometric shape in a single corner, crisp and perfectly legible, no drop shadows on the text (they muddy edges at small sizes and read as cheap), no watermarks.

ASPECT RATIO: 1:1 (1080×1080), square, Instagram-ready, high resolution.

promptText:
SUBJECT / FOCAL POINT: [PRODUCT, e.g. a chilled glass beverage bottle], centered as the unambiguous focal subject, photographed in warm, low-angle golden-hour sun (the sun near the horizon, roughly within an hour of sunset, color temperature in the 3000–3500K range) with rich directional shadow. Realistic condensation droplets and specular highlights on the surface where the material calls for it, crisp, clean product edges with no melted or warped geometry.

COMPOSITION: Golden hour's low, raking light angle naturally rim-lights and separates a product from its background without any extra lighting rig — the same reason product and lifestyle advertising shoots are so often scheduled around that one-hour window. Headline placement in the top third matches how a scroller's eye moves through a vertical feed ad — top-down, in roughly a second — so the hook has to land before the product image has even finished registering. Set [SETTING, e.g. a sandy beach with a calm ocean horizon and soft palm-frond shadows falling across the scene] behind the product — atmospheric and mood-setting, but deliberately secondary; a shallow depth of field (equivalent to roughly f/2.8 on a full-frame lens) softly blurs it so there's zero ambiguity about where the eye should land first. Compose the product on or near a rule-of-thirds intersection rather than dead-center-and-static.

LIGHTING & COLOR CONTRAST: Warm directional golden-hour glow with a gentle rim light separating the product from the background, long soft shadows reinforcing the time-of-day mood. Golden hour is a reliably high-performing color temperature for lifestyle and product advertising precisely because warm light reads as appetizing and inviting in a way cooler, flatter daylight doesn't. Vibrant, cinematic color grade, high contrast, premium advertising finish — not a flat, evenly-lit product-catalog shot.

TYPOGRAPHY / TEXT: Bold headline '[YOUR HEADLINE, e.g. FEEL THE SUNSHINE]' in a clean, bold, white sans-serif across the top third — high-contrast against the warm background so it stays legible even at reduced device brightness or in muted autoplay, where most social video is actually watched. Keep it short: headlines that resolve in under a second consistently outperform longer copy at ad-thumbnail scale. Because this prompt renders real headline copy, prefer gpt-image or Ideogram for cleaner type if the headline runs more than a couple of words — both have materially stronger text-rendering fidelity than Midjourney, which remains the least reliable of the major tools for on-image text; if Midjourney is used, keep the headline to one or two words and inspect the render closely before shipping. Reserve a small, clean logo slot near the bottom, kept empty — never invent a logo.

BACKGROUND: [SETTING], warm and atmospheric, softly blurred behind the product, free of clutter or distracting secondary props.

ASPECT RATIO: 4:5 (1080×1350) — the aspect ratio that survives Meta/Instagram feed cropping best for a product-forward ad, cropping far more gracefully than a 1:1 or 16:9 source would. Photorealistic, ultra sharp, 4k. Text-to-image, no photo upload needed — works in Midjourney, Nano Banana, Ideogram, or gpt-image; swap in an image-reference model instead if exact product packaging needs to be reproduced faithfully, and keep the output explicitly at --ar 4:5.

A cohesive color palette across every single prop under soft natural daylight, with gentle realistic shadows and zero off-palette items breaking the story

A semi-transparent off-white panel across the lower third holding a bold title and subtitle rendered directly as legible text in a strong dark sans-serif, with enough opacity to guarantee contrast against whatever's behind it

Fill in [FLAT-LAY ITEMS], [SURFACE], [PALETTE], and [YOUR TITLE]; keep the output at 4:5 explicitly, and double-check the rendered title/subtitle spelling before using
promptText:
TECHNICAL REFERENCE (flat-lay / knolling photography): the shot logic is directly overhead ("bird's eye"/knolling), captured at roughly a 50mm-equivalent focal length so prop shapes stay true — wide lenses barrel-distort the edges of a flat lay. Stop down to around f/8-f/11 so every prop reads sharp corner to corner rather than just the center, and light with one large diffused source overhead (a softbox, or open shade from a north-facing window with a scrim) so shadows fall soft and consistent in a single direction, not the multi-directional shadows a ring light produces. Composition leans on the 60-30-10 color rule (one dominant palette color at roughly 60% of the visual weight, a secondary at 30%, an accent at 10%) plus an odd-number/implied-triangle grouping principle borrowed from editorial still-life styling — both applied below.

SUBJECT / FOCAL POINT: [FLAT-LAY ITEMS, e.g. autumn essentials such as a notebook, a coffee cup, a folded sweater, and a few dried leaves], photographed as a photorealistic top-down flat lay on a [SURFACE, e.g. warm wooden tabletop] — shot directly overhead as if knolled for an editorial still-life, the props themselves the primary visual subject.

COMPOSITION: An odd number of props (three or five reads more natural than an even count), arranged along an implied triangle or diagonal flow with clear negative space between each one — never touching, never symmetrical-to-the-pixel. Every prop should read clearly in its full silhouette from directly above, with no overlap that obscures shape. Reserve the lower third for the text panel below; keep props out of that zone entirely rather than letting the panel crop them.

LIGHTING & COLOR CONTRAST: Apply the 60-30-10 rule — [PALETTE, e.g. warm rust and cream] as the dominant 60%, a secondary tone at 30%, one accent color at 10% — so nothing off-palette snags the eye. Light as one large diffused overhead source: soft, even, shadowless-to-gently-directional, no harsh hotspots that would blow out prop detail or fight the text panel's legibility.

TYPOGRAPHY / TEXT: A clean, semi-transparent off-white panel across the lower third — opaque enough to guarantee contrast against whatever prop or shadow falls behind it — holding a bold title '[YOUR TITLE, e.g. 5 THINGS TO TRY]' in a strong, dark, geometric sans-serif (think a Futura/Montserrat weight, not a script), plus a smaller subtitle line beneath it in a lighter weight of the same family. Both need to stay crisp and legible at feed-thumbnail scale — rendered text on a photographic scene is one of the harder combinations for image models, so treat tool choice as a first decision: prefer gpt-image or Ideogram, both materially stronger at this combination; Nano Banana can work with iteration; Midjourney is the weakest of the major tools here and a real risk on panel copy of this length. Double-check the rendered title/subtitle spelling before using, whichever tool is used.

BACKGROUND: The [SURFACE] itself, kept simple and evenly lit beneath the props — avoid messy overlap, off-palette colors, harsh directional shadows, or watermarks.

ASPECT RATIO: 4:5 (1080x1350), premium Instagram carousel cover. Photorealistic, high detail, 4k, balanced, editorial, breathable.

PLATFORM PARAMETERS: Midjourney --ar 4:5 --v 6.1 --style raw --stylize 250 --no clutter, harsh shadows, misspelled text, warped text; Ideogram — aspect ratio 4:5, Magic Prompt off to keep palette control, rendering quality set to "Quality" for the text panel; gpt-image — size 1024x1536 cropped to 4:5, quality "high". Nano Banana (Gemini) can iterate toward this but expect 2-3 passes to lock the title spelling.

description: A clean, legible 1:1 tip graphic with a number badge, headline, one supporting line, and a matching flat icon.
whatYouGet: Square 1:1 tip graphic with a clear scan order — bold circular number badge ('01') first, then your tip title as the dominant headline, matching how feed viewers actually process infographic tiles

One supporting body line beneath the headline plus exactly one flat-line icon on the right, matching your brand accent color with consistent stroke weight — built to repeat cleanly across a numbered series
Clean grid alignment with generous whitespace and a strict one-icon, one-badge rule, so nothing competes with the headline for the first glance
